variants.name: Guarded statement through a SQL client (libpqxx / SQLite)
variants.idiom_name: pqxx::result::affected_rows() / sqlite3_changes() on UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?
variants.implementation_notes: The classic form in C++ is the guarded statement issued through a SQL client: keep the version the session read, run the conditional UPDATE inside one RAII-scoped transaction (pqxx::work or a sqlite3 BEGIN), and decide the outcome from the affected-row count - pqxx::result::affected_rows() for libpqxx, sqlite3_changes() when using the SQLite C API from C++. RAII is what makes the discipline natural: the transaction object rolls back on the conflict path, so a thrown error cannot leave the system transaction open.
pitfalls: The check is only atomic because it is in the statement; issuing SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and then a separate UPDATE turns the pattern into a pessimistic lock (and costs a lock for the whole session if the transaction stays open).
Affected rows must be read from the same result/connection immediately - a logging query or another statement in between overwrites the count.
An exception thrown between the statement and COMMIT must not skip the rollback: the RAII transaction object handles this, hand-written COMMIT/ROLLBACK pairs do not.

variants.name: In-process compare-exchange retry loop
variants.implementation_notes: For shared state that never leaves the process the same validate-then-act mechanics reduce to a CAS loop: the value you read is the expected one, compare_exchange_weak publishes the new value only if the slot still holds it, and a failure hands back the current value so the loop can recompute. Use it for the in-memory form of an edit session; it replaces nothing at the persistence level, where the token must be a real column.
pitfalls: compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously: the loop must recompute from the updated expected value, not treat every failure as a real conflict.
The comparison is bitwise over the object representation, so padding/trap bits or multiple representations of one value (NaN) can make the exchange fail forever.
A CAS loop only relocates contention: under heavy conflict it burns CPU where a mutex or the database token would be cheaper.
